"Marking" as a noun connects to a single simple idea: something that marks. But "marking" can refer to either a visible mark itself (something you can see and point to) or the activity of making marks. This gives the word its different meanings across different contexts.
Sense 1 — A Visible Sign, Pattern, or Design on a Surface

This is the most universal and widely-used meaning. A marking (very often used in the plural: markings) is any visible sign, symbol, pattern, or design on the surface of something — whether painted, printed, stamped, or naturally occurring.

On animals

The natural color patterns on an animal's body are called its markings. A tiger's black stripes are its markings. A leopard's spots are its markings. The red patch on a robin's chest is one of its most distinctive markings. "Markings" here refers to the natural designs that give each species — or even each individual animal — its appearance and help tell one apart from another.

On roads

The painted lines, arrows, and symbols on road surfaces are called road markings. The white line dividing lanes is a road marking. The stripes at a zebra crossing are road markings. These markings communicate rules and guide everyone using the road.

On objects and packages

Products, packages, and equipment often carry markings — printed symbols, codes, arrows, or warnings. The word "fragile" on a box is a marking. The serial number stamped on a machine is a marking. Warning symbols on a chemical container are markings. Any visible label or sign placed on an object to convey information can be called a marking.

On maps and diagrams

Symbols, lines, and labels on a map are also markings. A dotted line representing a border, or a small cross indicating a church — these are markings on a map.
Sense 2 — The Activity of Correcting and Grading Student Work

This sense is especially common in British, Indian, Australian, and most Commonwealth English, and it appears constantly in educational settings.

When a teacher reads through students' assignments, tests, or essays — checking them, writing comments, and assigning scores — that whole activity is called marking. It is used as an uncountable noun here, meaning it describes a task or activity rather than individual items.

  • "She had a huge pile of marking to finish before Monday."
  • "Teachers often spend their evenings on marking."
  • "The marking of exam papers must be completed within two weeks."

A related phrase you'll often see: a marking scheme — a guide prepared in advance that tells a teacher exactly which answers are correct and how many points each answer deserves. Teachers use marking schemes to ensure consistent, fair grading.

Note on American English: In the United States, this same activity is usually called grading, not marking. Both words describe the same thing — evaluating student work and assigning scores.

Also worth knowing: marking is the activity, not the result. The result — the score or grade a student receives — is called a mark (in British English) or a grade (in American English). So the teacher does the marking; the student gets a mark.
Sense 3 — The Process of Placing Marks on Something

In a more general sense, "marking" can refer to the process of putting marks on something for identification, measurement, labeling, or organization. This is often formal or technical language.

  • "The marking of the cattle was done with a hot iron brand."
  • "Careful marking of the boundaries prevented land disputes later."
  • "The marking of the fabric before cutting is essential for a clean result."

In this sense, "marking" is typically uncountable — it describes an action or process, not a specific visible mark.
Sense 4 — In Sports: Closely Guarding an Opponent

In team sports like football (soccer), rugby, and hockey, marking is the defensive technique of staying close to an opposing player to stop them from receiving the ball or creating danger.

  • "His marking of the opposing striker was tight and disciplined all game."
  • "Good marking is essential when defending set pieces."
  • "The team's marking was poor in the second half, which is why they conceded."

Here, "marking" describes both the act and the quality of guarding or covering an opponent. When someone is described as doing "tight marking" or "poor marking," it refers to how closely and effectively they stayed with their opponent.
Singular vs. Plural — A Crucial Distinction

Understanding when to say "marking," "a marking," or "markings" makes a real difference.

"A marking" (singular, countable) — one specific, individual mark or pattern:

  • "There was a strange marking on the wall."
  • "The technician noticed an unusual marking on the component."

"Markings" (plural, countable) — a collection or set of marks or patterns:

  • "The snake had bright yellow markings along its back."
  • "The road markings in this area were faded and hard to see."

This plural form is the most common when describing patterns on animals, roads, aircraft, or objects.

"Marking" (uncountable, used without "a" or a number) — an activity or process:

  • "The marking was finished by Friday." (= the grading work)
  • "The marking of the survey plot took three hours." (= the process of placing marks)

• Road markings — painted signs and lines on roads
  • Animal markings — natural patterns of color on an animal
  • Marking scheme — a teacher's guide for grading student work consistently
  • Tight marking / close marking — defending very closely in sports
  • Pile of marking — a stack of student work waiting to be graded
  • Marking criteria — the standards used to judge and grade work

"Marking" as a noun has four main areas of meaning:

  1. A visible sign, pattern, or design on a surface — the most universal meaning. Road markings, animal markings, markings on packages all fall here. The plural "markings" is especially common.
  2. The activity of correcting and grading student work — central to education, especially in British and Commonwealth English.
  3. The process of placing marks on something — for identification, measurement, or organization.
  4. In sports: closely guarding an opponent — a key defensive concept in team sports.

The first two are the meanings you are most likely to encounter in everyday life. The word "markings" (plural) is particularly frequent when describing natural or painted patterns, and "marking" (uncountable) is the standard word British and Indian English speakers use for a teacher's most time-consuming task.
